unit.title: Prepare dishes using basic methods of cookery

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Explain the difference between moist heat, dry heat and fat-based methods of cookery. Give two methods and one Jamaican or international dish for each.
essays.modelAnswer: Moist heat methods cook food in water, stock, steam or other liquid. The food cannot go above about 100 °C, so it does not brown, but it becomes tender. Examples are boiling, used for green bananas and dumplings, simmering, stewing for curry goat, poaching for eggs, and steaming for steamed fish with okra. Dry heat methods cook food with hot air or direct heat, without liquid. The food browns on the outside and gets more flavour. Examples are roasting, as with roast chicken or roast breadfruit, baking, as with bread, rum cake or bun, and grilling, as with jerk chicken. Fat-based methods cook food in hot oil or fat, which gets much hotter than water, so the food cooks quickly and becomes crisp and brown. Examples are shallow frying, for fried plantain, deep frying, for escovitch fish or festival, and sautéing or stir-frying, for ackee and saltfish or vegetables.
markingPoints: Moist heat: water, stock or steam; tender, no browning
Two moist methods with a dish (for example boiling, stewing, steaming)
Dry heat: hot air or direct heat; browning and flavour; two methods with a dish
Fat-based: hot oil or fat, quick, crisp; two methods with a dish
Examples are correct and include Jamaican dishes

essays.stem: Describe how you would prepare and cook brown stew chicken, including the food safety checks you would make.
essays.modelAnswer: I wash my hands, put on a clean apron and hat, and get my mise en place ready. I take the chicken from the fridge, using the board kept for raw meat, cut it into pieces and trim excess fat. I season it with salt, black pepper, garlic, onion, thyme, scallion and a little browning, and leave it covered in the fridge to marinate. I wash my hands and clean the board after handling raw chicken. I heat a little oil in a heavy pot, such as a Dutch pot, and brown the chicken on all sides to give colour and flavour, then remove it. I fry the onions, sweet pepper and tomato, put the chicken back, add a little water or stock to come part way up, and cover the pot. I simmer it gently, stirring now and then, until the chicken is tender and the sauce is thick. I check the core temperature of the thickest piece with a clean probe: it must reach about 74 °C. I taste and adjust the seasoning, and keep it hot at 63 °C or above until it is served.
markingPoints: Hygiene and mise en place; raw meat board, hands washed after raw chicken
Seasons and marinates the chicken, kept covered in the fridge
Browns the chicken in a heavy pot for colour and flavour
Adds vegetables and liquid, covers and simmers slowly until tender
Probes to about 74 °C, tastes, and holds at 63 °C or above

essays.stem: Describe how you would deep fry fish for escovitch fish safely, from preparing the fryer to serving.
essays.modelAnswer: I check that the fryer or deep pot is clean and dry, and fill it with fresh oil only to the fill line, never more than about half full in a pot. I heat it to the temperature in the recipe, often about 170 to 190 °C, using the thermostat or a thermometer, as the maker's guide says. I clean and scale the fish, score it, season it, and pat it dry with paper towels so that the oil does not spit. I coat it lightly in seasoned flour and shake off the extra. I lower the fish into the oil gently, away from me, using a basket or tongs, and I do not overfill the fryer, so the oil stays hot. I fry it until it is crisp and golden and the flesh flakes at the bone. I lift it out, drain it on paper towels and top it with the hot pickled sauce of vinegar, onion, carrot and scotch bonnet. I never leave the fryer, never put water near it, and keep a fire blanket close. I turn it off and let it cool before cleaning.
markingPoints: Checks the fryer; fills only to the line; heats to about 170–190 °C as the maker says
Cleans, seasons and dries the fish; light flour coating
Lowers food gently away from the body; does not overload
Cooks until golden and done; drains and adds the escovitch sauce
Fire safety: never leaves it, no water, fire blanket nearby, cools before cleaning

essays.stem: Explain how you would steam fish or vegetables, and why steaming is a healthy method of cookery.
essays.modelAnswer: I put a little water in the bottom of a pot or steamer and bring it to the boil, making sure the water does not touch the basket. I prepare the food: for steamed fish, I clean and season the fish and place it on a plate or in the basket with sliced okra, onion, thyme, scallion and pimento; for vegetables, such as callaloo, carrot or pumpkin, I wash and cut them into even pieces so they cook at the same time. I put the food in the basket above the boiling water, cover it with a tight lid and keep the water boiling. I check that the water does not boil dry. I lift the lid away from my face to avoid steam burns. The fish is done when the flesh is white and flakes easily; the vegetables are done when tender but still bright in colour. Steaming is healthy because no fat is added, and fewer vitamins are lost into the water than in boiling, so the food keeps more of its goodness, colour and shape.
markingPoints: Water boiling below the food, not touching it; tight lid
Food prepared: cleaned, seasoned, cut evenly
Checks water level; lifts the lid away from the face
Knows when it is done (fish flakes; vegetables tender and bright)
Healthy: no added fat, fewer vitamins lost, keeps colour and shape

essays.stem: Describe how you would roast a whole chicken, and how you would know it is cooked and ready to serve.
essays.modelAnswer: I preheat the oven to the temperature in the recipe, often about 180 to 200 °C. I take the chicken from the fridge, remove any giblets, and handle it only on the raw meat board, washing my hands afterwards. I season it inside and out, rub it with a little oil or butter, and can put onion, garlic and thyme inside. I place it on a rack or on sliced onions in a roasting tray so that the heat goes all round it. I roast it, basting it every 20 to 30 minutes with the hot fat and juices so that it stays moist and browns evenly. I check that it is cooked by putting a clean probe thermometer into the thickest part of the thigh, away from the bone: it must reach about 74 °C, or as the Centre's food safety plan says. The juices should run clear, not pink. I let it rest for about 10 to 15 minutes, covered loosely, so that the juices settle, then I carve it and serve it on a hot plate, or hold it at 63 °C or above.
markingPoints: Preheats the oven; handles raw chicken hygienically
Seasons and oils it; places it on a rack or vegetables in a tray
Bastes during roasting
Probes the thickest part to about 74 °C; juices run clear
Rests before carving; serves hot or holds at 63 °C or above

essays.stem: Explain the food safety rules a cook must follow when cooking, holding and cooling hot food.
essays.modelAnswer: Germs grow fastest in the danger zone, between about 5 °C and 63 °C, so food must spend as little time there as possible. Raw food is kept in the fridge at 5 °C or below until it is needed, and raw meat is stored on the bottom shelf, away from ready-to-eat food. Separate colour-coded boards, knives and cloths are used for raw and cooked food, and hands are washed after handling raw meat. Food must be cooked right through: poultry and minced meat should reach a core temperature of about 74 °C, checked with a clean probe thermometer, or as the Centre's food safety plan says. Hot food for service is held at 63 °C or above. Food to be kept is cooled quickly, by spreading it in shallow trays, using an ice bath or a blast chiller, and then covered, labelled with the date and put in the fridge. Leftovers are reheated only once, until piping hot. Stock is rotated: first in, first out.
markingPoints: Danger zone 5–63 °C; keep food out of it
Cold storage at 5 °C or below; raw meat on the bottom shelf
Separate boards and hand washing to stop cross-contamination
Core temperature about 74 °C for poultry and mince; hot-hold at 63 °C or above
Cool quickly in shallow trays, cover, label, date, FIFO; reheat once only

essays.stem: Describe how you would prepare ackee and saltfish safely, from preparing the ackee and saltfish to serving.
essays.modelAnswer: I soak the saltfish in cold water for some hours or overnight, changing the water, or I boil it and throw the water away, then taste a piece to check that most of the salt is gone. I remove the skin and bones and flake the fish. For fresh ackee, I use only pods that have opened naturally on the tree; closed or forced pods are not safe. I remove the black seeds and the pink membrane from each piece, because they are poisonous, and wash the yellow flesh. I boil the ackee in salted water until just tender, then drain it and throw the water away. If I use canned ackee, I drain it. In a pan I sauté onion, garlic, scallion, thyme, sweet pepper and tomato in a little oil, add the flaked saltfish, and then fold in the ackee gently so that it does not break up. I season with black pepper and a little scotch bonnet if wanted, heat it through, taste it and serve it hot with fried dumplings, festival, boiled green bananas or roast breadfruit.
markingPoints: Soaks or boils the saltfish to remove salt; removes skin and bones
Uses only naturally opened ackee pods
Removes the seeds and pink membrane; boils and discards the water
Sautés seasonings, adds saltfish, folds in ackee gently
Tastes, serves hot with suitable sides

essays.stem: Explain the main hazards when cooking in a kitchen and how a cook keeps safe from each one.
essays.modelAnswer: Burns and scalds come from hot pans, ovens, oil, steam and boiling liquids. I use dry oven cloths, turn pan handles inwards, lift lids away from my face and never leave hot oil unattended. Cuts come from knives and equipment. I use the right knife, keep it sharp, cut on a steady board, carry knives point down, never try to catch a falling knife and wash knives separately. Slips happen on wet or greasy floors, so I wipe spills at once, use a wet floor sign and wear non-slip shoes. Fire can start from hot oil or a gas leak. I never put water on burning oil; I turn off the heat and cover it with a lid or fire blanket. If I smell gas, I turn off the supply if safe, open windows, use no flames or switches and report it. Pressure cookers are used as the maker's instructions say, and opened only when the pressure has dropped. Guards stay on mixers and slicers. I follow the Centre's rules and report any accident.
markingPoints: Burns and scalds: dry cloths, handles in, lids away from face
Knives: right knife, sharp, carry point down, never catch a falling knife
Slips: wipe spills, wet floor sign, non-slip shoes
Fire and gas: no water on oil, lid or fire blanket; gas leak actions
Pressure cooker and machine guards per the maker; report accidents

essays.stem: You must serve roast chicken, steamed vegetables and rice and peas together at 12:30. Explain how you would plan the work so that everything is ready and hot at the same time.
essays.modelAnswer: First I read each recipe and find out how long each dish takes: the chicken needs the longest, about one and a half hours with resting, the rice and peas about 45 minutes if the peas are already cooked, and the steamed vegetables only about 10 minutes. I work backwards from 12:30 and write a simple time plan. I do my mise en place first: I collect and weigh the ingredients, wash and cut the vegetables, season the chicken and cook or soak the peas. I preheat the oven and put the chicken in at about 11:00. While it roasts, I start the rice and peas at about 11:40. At about 12:10 I take out the chicken, check it with a probe and let it rest. At about 12:15 I steam the vegetables, so they stay bright and crisp. I warm the plates, then carve the chicken and plate everything at 12:30. Planning saves time, stops food overcooking or going cold, and keeps the kitchen calm.
markingPoints: Reads recipes and works out the cooking time of each dish
Works backwards from the serving time to make a time plan
Does the mise en place first
Starts the longest dish first and the quickest last; rests the meat
Warms plates and serves together; says why planning matters

essays.stem: Explain how a cook can tell when food is cooked properly by different methods, and how to present it well.
essays.modelAnswer: Boiled or steamed vegetables are done when a knife goes in easily but they are still bright in colour and keep their shape; overcooked vegetables are soft, dull and lose vitamins. Pasta should be al dente, firm to the bite. Rice and peas is ready when the water is absorbed and the grains are tender and separate. Fish is cooked when the flesh turns white, is no longer see-through and flakes easily. Chicken and minced meat must reach a core temperature of about 74 °C, checked with a clean probe, and the juices run clear. Fried food is golden and crisp, not pale or burnt, and is drained well. Cakes are done when a skewer comes out clean. To present food well, I serve hot food on warm, clean plates and cold food on cold plates. I arrange the food neatly, with the main item at the front, add a little colour, such as a sprig of thyme or a slice of tomato, and wipe the rim of the plate before it leaves the kitchen.
markingPoints: Vegetables tender but bright; pasta al dente; rice tender and separate
Fish white and flaking; chicken probed to about 74 °C, juices clear
Fried food golden, crisp and drained; cakes tested with a skewer
Hot plates for hot food, cold for cold; neat arrangement
Garnish for colour and a clean plate rim

practical1.title: Moist heat methods: brown stew chicken, steamed callaloo and boiled food
practical1.brief: Your group will cook a Jamaican lunch for six using moist heat methods: brown stew chicken (browned, then stewed slowly in a covered pot), steamed callaloo with onion and tomato, and boiled food (green bananas, yam and spinners or flour dumplings). Share the work so that every member takes part in each stage: one or two members lead each dish, and every member must season and cook at least part of one dish, check a core or holding temperature with a clean probe thermometer and record it, and take part in plating and the clean-down. Write a simple time plan before you start so that all three dishes are ready and hot at the same time. Present six plates and one sample plate for the assessor. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and the time plan and temperature record to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Chicken pieces (about 1.5 kg), onion, garlic, scallion, thyme, sweet pepper, tomato, browning, salt, black pepper, oil
Green bananas, yellow or white yam, flour and salt for dumplings
Heavy-based pot (such as a Dutch pot), saucepans, a steamer or pot with a basket, and lids
Colour-coded boards and knives, probe thermometer and sanitising wipes
Warm plates, a temperature record sheet and a time plan sheet
Fire blanket and first aid kit in the kitchen
photos: Mise en place: all ingredients and equipment ready, members in clean uniform
Chicken browning in the heavy pot
Callaloo in the steamer above boiling water
Green bananas, yam and dumplings boiling
A probe thermometer in the chicken, with the reading recorded
checklist: Washed hands and wore clean uniform, with hair covered
Used the right colour-coded board and knife, and kept raw and cooked food apart
Seasoned and cooked at least part of one dish by the correct moist heat method
Controlled the heat correctly: browning, then simmering, then steaming and boiling
Checked and recorded a core temperature of about 74 °C, or a holding temperature of 63 °C or above
Tasted with a clean spoon and adjusted the seasoning
Plated neatly on warm plates with clean rims
Worked safely and helped clean and sanitise equipment and surfaces
safety: Turn pan handles inwards, use dry oven cloths and lift lids away from your face
Use the right knife, carry knives point down and never try to catch a falling knife
Wipe spills at once and put out a wet floor sign
Keep raw chicken apart from ready-to-eat food; wash hands after handling it
Know where the fire blanket and first aid kit are; follow the Centre's rules for gas and stoves

practical2.title: Dry heat and frying methods: oven-roast jerk chicken, fried fish and festival, sautéed vegetables
practical2.brief: Your group will cook a lunch for six using dry heat and fat-based methods: jerk-seasoned chicken roasted in the oven (or grilled, if the Centre has a safe outdoor grill), shallow-fried or deep-fried fish, festival (deep fried), and sautéed mixed vegetables. Before you start, write a time plan and agree the fryer temperature with the assessor, as the fryer maker's guide says. Every member must take part in each stage: every member seasons or prepares at least one item, cooks at least one item by a dry heat or frying method while the assessor watches, checks and records a core temperature with a clean probe, and helps with plating and the clean-down. Present six plates and one sample plate for the assessor. Photograph each stage below and add the photos, the time plan and the temperature record to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the kitchen is clean and the cooled oil is stored or disposed of as the Centre's rules say.
materials: Chicken leg quarters (about 1.5 kg) and jerk seasoning (scotch bonnet, pimento, scallion, thyme, garlic)
Whole fish or fish fillets, flour, salt and black pepper
Flour, cornmeal, sugar, baking powder and salt for festival
Carrots, sweet peppers, cabbage, onion and a little oil for sautéing
Oven and roasting trays, deep fryer or deep pot with a thermometer, frying pan or wok, tongs and a spider or basket
Colour-coded boards and knives, gloves for handling scotch bonnet, a probe thermometer, paper towels
Fire blanket and a suitable fire extinguisher near the fryer
photos: Mise en place, with gloves worn for the scotch bonnet
Chicken seasoned and in the oven (or on the grill)
Fryer oil at the agreed temperature, shown on the thermometer
Fish being lowered gently into the oil, away from the body
Festival frying and draining on paper towels
Vegetables being sautéed in a hot pan
A probe thermometer in the chicken, with the reading recorded
The six finished plates and the clean kitchen
checklist: Wore clean uniform, washed hands and wore gloves when handling scotch bonnet
Used the right board and knife; kept raw and cooked food apart
Cooked at least one item by a dry heat or frying method correctly
Dried food before frying and lowered it gently away from the body
Kept the fryer at the agreed temperature and never left it unattended
Checked and recorded a core temperature of about 74 °C for the chicken
Drained fried food well and plated it neatly on warm plates
Cleaned down safely, letting the oil cool fully first
safety: Never leave hot oil; never let water near it; fill fryers only to the line
If oil catches fire, turn off the heat and cover it with a lid or fire blanket; never use water
Wear gloves for scotch bonnet and do not touch your eyes
Use dry oven cloths, turn handles inwards and keep the floor clean and dry
Let oil cool fully before moving or straining it; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
